items.prompt: What is a design token?
choices: A named value, such as a color, defined only once
A finished button that already includes its disabled state
A mockup of one screen shared as an image file
A written report listing every bug found in an audit
items.explanation: A token is a name standing in for a value, defined once so screens reference it instead of retyping it.

items.prompt: Which layer is built out of tokens?
choices: The shoppers' account and purchase history records
The backend database that stores the whole product catalog
The component library, such as Button, Input and Card
The marketing campaign calendar for the next quarter
items.explanation: Components consume tokens for color, radius and spacing, then screens assemble components.

items.prompt: Referring to `color.primary` instead of typing a hex code means using a...
choices: screen
token
sprint
mockup
items.explanation: A name that stands for a shared value is a token.

items.prompt: A Button that already knows its color, radius and disabled state is a...
choices: token
wireframe
palette
component
items.explanation: It bundles tokens plus behavior into one reusable piece.

items.prompt: What does 'single source of truth' mean for a blue?
choices: Every squad keeps its own copy and compares them yearly
It is defined in one place and everything else points at it
Whoever built the screen first decides the blue for everyone
The newest screen always overrides the older screens' blue
items.explanation: One definition, many references, no redefinitions.

items.prompt: Which description fits a design system best?
choices: Tokens, components and the rules keeping them authoritative
A folder of screenshots of every screen in the shipped app today
A list of colors the brand team once approved on paper
A single large Figma page with every possible button
items.explanation: The system includes values, reusable pieces and the process that keeps them authoritative.

items.prompt: What do product screens get assembled from?
choices: Raw hex codes typed fresh by each engineer on each screen
Screenshots exported from last quarter's audit
Components that were themselves built from tokens
Separate buttons redrawn by each squad in turn
items.explanation: Screens sit at the top of the chain: tokens, then components, then screens.

items.prompt: Where do design decisions move once a system exists?
choices: Downstream, to each engineer building a single screen
Sideways, to whichever squad ships its screen first
Out of the process, since the system makes them for you
Upstream, to one decision that many screens reference
items.explanation: Pick the primary blue once, instead of once per button.

items.prompt: A team has a 30-page style guide and a polished design file, yet engineers type hex codes from memory. Is this a design system?
choices: Yes; once the values are documented and approved, the team has a real system
Yes, as long as the guide and the design file agree with each other
No; code never imports the shared values, so the guide only documents one
No; a system needs at least a hundred components before it counts as one
items.explanation: A system is the thing code consumes. Without an imported source, documents and designs just describe values people can still mistype.
items.reference:
Three layers
🧱 tokens: named values
🧩 components: built from tokens
📱 screens: assembled from components
📌 system = all of it + the rules
Why: a system is the thing engineers import, so one definition serves every screen.
items.learnMore:
A system is used, not read

Tokens and components only count as a system when product code actually imports them. Documentation that describes the values without being the values is a record of intent, not a source of truth.

Common mistake

Treating a style-guide PDF or a design file as the system itself.
items.reflection: Think of any shared thing at home or work (a recipe, a template, a house rule). Is it the one source everyone uses, or a description people copy from memory?

items.prompt: Which statement separates a token from a component correctly?
choices: A token is a whole screen; a component is one single color used on it
A token is a named value; a component adds behavior to bundled tokens
A component is a named value; a token adds the behavior on top of it
They are one thing under two names, one used by design and one by code
items.explanation: Tokens are inputs (a color, a radius). Components are finished pieces that consume them and add behavior such as a disabled state.

items.prompt: What is visual drift?
choices: Small, uncoordinated deviations that add up to inconsistency
A smooth animation that slides content across the whole screen
A planned redesign that updates every screen at once
A browser setting that shifts colors on older monitors
items.explanation: Drift is accumulated small differences nobody coordinated.

items.prompt: What makes drift grow in an app?
choices: A smaller team that talks to each other every single day
Using one component library for every screen in the app
More screens and more people with no shared source of truth
Having a written reference that everyone is able to import easily
items.explanation: Each extra screen or person is another independent chance to deviate.

items.prompt: Is drift mainly caused by careless designers?
choices: Yes; it happens only when someone ignores the brand rules
No; values copied from memory drift even for careful people
Yes; it appears only in teams with very little design experience
No; it is caused by monitors rendering colors differently
items.explanation: The cause is structural, so careful people still produce it.

items.prompt: Which of these is not really a design system?
choices: A token package that every squad imports
A Button component published as a versioned library
Tokens and components with a review process for changes
A style-guide PDF that nobody opens
items.explanation: If code does not import it, it documents a system rather than being one.

items.prompt: The audit found several blues for 'primary'. That is evidence of...
choices: a brand that deliberately uses many blues
no single source of truth for the value
one squad having poor eyesight for color
too many shoppers visiting the app at once
items.explanation: Many versions of one value means no one place defines it.

items.prompt: What minimum contrast does WCAG AA ask for normal-size text?
items.explanation: AA asks at least 4.5 : 1 for normal text, which is why 3.68 : 1 on the checkout button falls short.

items.prompt: How can the 'pick a blue for this button' decision repeated 40 times be improved?
choices: Let each squad pick its own blue, then compare them yearly
Ask the newest hire to choose a blue for each screen
Decide the primary blue once and reference it everywhere
Repeat the decision, but write the result in a document
items.explanation: One decision referenced many times beats many decisions.

items.prompt: Where does a color value live when drift occurs?
choices: In one token that every screen references by name
In a versioned package that components are built from
In a single file that all squads are required to import
In people's memory and in hex codes copied by hand
items.explanation: With no shared reference, the value is recalled or copied, so it drifts.

items.prompt: Every Northwind designer is careful, yet an audit finds six blues. Why?
choices: Careful designers still choose a different brand color for each screen on purpose
Screens render differently on each phone, which makes one blue look like six
Each screen recalls the value alone, with no common reference to check against
The audit tool counts one blue several times when it appears in several files
items.explanation: Drift needs no sloppiness: independent recall on every screen is enough to produce it.
items.reference:
Where drift comes from
🧠 value kept in memory
📋 hex code copied by hand
🔁 repeated on every new screen
📈 more screens + more people = more drift
Why: no shared reference means every screen is a fresh chance to recall the value slightly wrong.
items.learnMore:
Drift is structural

Careful people still produce drift when the value lives in heads and copied codes. Each screen is an independent recall, and the odds of a mismatch grow with the number of screens and the number of people.

Common mistake

Blaming the last person who touched the screen instead of the missing shared source.
items.reflection: Where in your own work does the same value get retyped by hand in several places, and what would the single shared reference be?

items.prompt: The design file shows one blue but the shipped app uses another. What failure is this?
choices: A rendering bug in the screen hardware of the phone used for the audit
Two sources of truth that disagree, since neither one references the other
An accessibility rule that forbids two screens from matching their blues
One token that was accidentally defined twice inside a single published token package
items.explanation: When design and code each hold their own value, nothing keeps them aligned.

The brand's primary blue must be wrong on every single screen in the app

items.prompt: A lead wants one reviewer to catch every visual deviation. What stays unchanged?
choices: The cause: no single place exists where each value is defined
The number of screens, which the reviewer is expected to reduce over time
The release speed, which becomes slower by a fixed factor per reviewer
The squads' freedom to retype values, which the review process now bans
items.explanation: A reviewer becomes the memory for the system. Remove the cause by creating the shared source, not by adding a human check.

items.prompt: Name the three token layers.
choices: Global, alias and component
Primary, secondary and tertiary
Light, dark and high-contrast
Draft, review and published
items.explanation: Global holds raw values, alias gives roles, component fills one slot.

items.prompt: Which layer holds raw values like `#2563EB`?
choices: Alias tokens
Component tokens
Global tokens
Screens
items.explanation: Global tokens are the plain palette with no stated purpose.

items.prompt: Which layer attaches a role such as 'primary' to a value?
choices: Global tokens
Alias tokens
Component tokens
Page layouts
items.explanation: An alias says what a value is for.

items.prompt: A component token should point at...
choices: a screenshot of the finished screen
a hex code typed directly into it
a different component's source file
an alias, not a raw value
items.explanation: Pointing at an alias keeps the chain intact.

items.prompt: `radius.md = 8px` belongs to which layer?
choices: Alias
Global
Component
Screen
items.explanation: It is a raw value with no role attached.

items.prompt: `button.background = color.primary` belongs to which layer?
choices: Component
Global
Alias
Foundation
items.explanation: It fills one slot of one component by pointing at an alias.

items.prompt: What does `color.primary` mean?
choices: A hex code that can never be changed after release
A button that is always colored the same blue
A role, resolving to whatever the global is now
A screen that appears first in the app
items.explanation: The name is a role, so what it resolves to can change.

items.prompt: Why have an alias layer between global and component?
choices: So designers can avoid learning the palette entirely
So every token has to be defined three separate times
So the app can run without loading any color at all in dark mode
So a role can move to a new value without editing components
items.explanation: Roles absorb change; components stay untouched.

items.prompt: Marketing wants only link text to move from the primary blue to teal; buttons stay blue. Which edit is right?
choices: Edit blue.500 to teal, so that every use of the primary blue changes together at once
Edit each screen's link color by hand and record the change in a shared file
Repoint the link component's token to a teal alias and leave blue.500 untouched
Delete color.primary so that links fall back to whatever default remains
items.explanation: blue.500 feeds every primary use, including buttons. Only the link's own slot should change.
items.reference:
Who points at whom
🧱 global: blue.500 = #2563EB
🏷️ alias: color.primary → blue.500
🧩 component: button.background → color.primary
👉 each layer points down, never skips
Why: each layer references the next one up, so a change is made once, at the right layer.
items.learnMore:
Meaning lives in the alias

Global tokens say what exists; alias tokens say what a color is for; component tokens say which slot uses it. Repointing an alias changes a role without touching the palette or the components.

Common mistake

Pointing a component token straight at a hex or a global, skipping the alias.
items.reflection: Pick something you rename rather than retype (a contact name, a folder). What would break if you hardcoded the raw value everywhere instead?

items.prompt: A component token is set to `#2563EB` directly. What goes wrong at the next rebrand?
choices: Nothing goes wrong, because its hex equals the global value today and forever
It skips the chain, so editing blue.500 never reaches that component
The whole alias layer is deleted when the build compiles that component
That component turns invisible until somebody repairs its token by hand
items.explanation: A hardcoded value is a hidden second source. It matches today and stays behind when the global changes.

items.prompt: `color.danger = red.500` is added for an urgent action. Which layer is it, and why there?
choices: Global; it is a raw value that happens to have one specific purpose
Component; it applies to exactly one button on exactly one screen
Screen; it describes where on the page the color will be displayed
Alias; it names a role (danger) over a global color
items.explanation: It states what the color is for and points at the raw red, which is the alias job.

choices: Global; an edit there fans out to every alias and component below it
Component; each edit there rewrites the entire palette for all of the screens
Alias; roles are meant to be rewritten each time a new feature ships
All three equally, since every layer reaches every screen in the same way
items.explanation: The more upstream the edit, the more it affects, so the raw palette changes only for a rebrand or major refresh.

items.prompt: How many token lines change for a primary-blue rebrand?
choices: One: the global value
Forty: one for each screen
Three: one for each layer
None: it needs a new app
items.explanation: Every layer downstream references the global.

items.prompt: What does dark mode swap in?
choices: A second set of components
A second copy of every screen
A second global palette
A second design team
items.explanation: Alias and component tokens resolve to the new palette values.

items.prompt: What do alias and component tokens do in dark mode?
choices: Get deleted and then rewritten by hand per screen
Resolve to new values with no code change
Stay frozen on their light values
Move into the screens themselves
items.explanation: They are references, so a new palette changes what they resolve to.

items.prompt: What forces every screen to use the whole token set correctly?
choices: A longer review checklist
A bigger color palette
A printed style guide
A component library
items.explanation: Components bundle the tokens so screens cannot skip any.

items.prompt: Do rebrands or dark mode need component code changes?
choices: Yes; every component file must be edited by hand
No; the chain resolves differently by itself
Yes, but only inside the checkout screens
Only when the app is first installed
items.explanation: The components reference tokens, not values.

items.prompt: Where should likely-to-change decisions be placed?
choices: As far upstream as possible
Inside each screen's own code
Inside every component's private file
In a reviewer's memory
items.explanation: Upstream means fewer places to change.

items.prompt: What does a tool like Style Dictionary do?
choices: Draws every screen of the app
Tests the whole checkout flow for bugs
Compiles the chain for each platform
Chooses the brand color for you
items.explanation: One authored chain can output web variables and native equivalents.

items.prompt: Why does a shared Button prevent a forgotten disabled state?
choices: Reviewers memorize each state for every screen
Engineers receive a reminder before each deadline
Disabled buttons are removed from the product
The disabled style ships inside the component
items.explanation: A screen using the component gets the state for free.

items.prompt: For dark mode, an engineer proposes editing every component's styles. What is the better design?
choices: Edit only the components on the screens that shoppers use most often each week
Duplicate every component with a dark version that sits beside the original
Swap the global palette once; aliases and components re-resolve with no edits
Disable dark mode on any screen that carries custom styles of its own
items.explanation: Dark mode is the rebrand trick again: change the upstream palette, not the consumers.
items.reference:
One upstream edit
🎨 rebrand: edit blue.500
🌙 dark mode: swap global palette
🏷️ aliases re-resolve
🧩 components re-resolve, 0 code edits
Why: decisions likely to change sit upstream, so one change replaces dozens of local ones.
items.learnMore:
Values vs consumption

Tokens supply values; components force every screen to use the full set together. A rebrand or theme swap works only for screens that consumed the chain rather than retyping it.

Common mistake

Assuming a token catalog alone prevents a forgotten disabled state.
items.reflection: Which decision in your own work changes often enough that it deserves a single upstream place?

items.prompt: Tokens are published but there is no Button component. A squad under deadline skips the disabled token. What addresses the cause?

Ship a Button with the disabled style built in, so skipping it is impossible
Publish more tokens so that the disabled state gets a larger number of names
Ask the squad to read the token documentation once more before the next deadline
items.explanation: Tokens make correctness possible; components make it the default.

choices: Whatever resolves through color.primary; direct users of blue.500 stay

items.prompt: The post-mortem decided the checkout bug was a...
choices: process failure, not a diligence failure
rare hardware fault in a few phones
deliberate design choice by the brand team
mistake that cannot happen again anywhere
items.explanation: Four independent implementations made it likely.

items.prompt: How many separate Button implementations existed?
choices: One, shared by all squads
Two, one per platform
Four, one per team
Forty, one per screen
items.explanation: Four teams had four implementations.

items.prompt: What does a review checklist rely on?
choices: The code compiling without any errors or warnings
People remembering to apply it each time
The tokens being published to a package
The app running on every device size
items.explanation: A checklist is a human reminder.

items.prompt: What does a shared component remove?
choices: The need for any visual design work
All of the squads' product decisions about features
The tokens that the component uses
The chance to rebuild the piece differently
items.explanation: One implementation is left to get right.

items.prompt: Which finding was a functional bug, not cosmetic?
choices: The several shades of primary blue
The checkout disabled-state failure
The varying corner radii
The choice of font size in a footer
items.explanation: It affected whether shoppers understood the button's state.

items.prompt: Six blues on 40 screens is evidence of...
choices: no single source of truth for the value
a shortage of screens in the whole product
a successful brand refresh in progress
an unusually large design team
items.explanation: Many versions means no one authoritative definition.

items.prompt: What structural question did the post-mortem ask first?
choices: Which engineer wrote the checkout button originally?
How many shoppers use the checkout screen?
Was there any one place defining a disabled button?
Which hex code is closest to the brand?
items.explanation: It looked for the missing source, not for blame.

items.prompt: Which kind of fix scales best?
choices: One that asks everyone to be much more careful in review
One that adds a longer meeting each week
One that names the person responsible
One that makes the mistake structurally harder to make
items.explanation: Structure holds under deadline pressure; memory does not.

items.prompt: Compare a stricter checklist with a shared Button. Which comparison is right?
choices: Both solve the problem equally once the whole team has been trained to use them
The checklist is the only option that keeps scaling as more squads are added
A checklist needs humans every time; a component leaves one version to get right

items.explanation: A checklist covers only what someone wrote down and needs perfect re-runs. A shared piece removes the failure mode on that axis.

items.prompt: What is the first rollout step?
choices: Extract tokens from the values already in use
Rewrite all 40 screens in one release
Hire a new design team from scratch
Delete the old buttons on every screen
items.explanation: Tokens can be shipped without touching a component.

items.prompt: Why ship tokens before components?
choices: They are always bigger than components
They are required by the app store
Nothing consumes them yet, so they cannot break anything
They replace the need for components
items.explanation: A package with no consumers is risk-free.

items.prompt: Which components come first?
choices: The rarest ones, to test the process
The ones with the most duplicated, drifted code
Whichever the newest hire prefers
Those that no screen currently uses
items.explanation: Button, Input and Card collided most.

items.prompt: How are old screens migrated?
choices: All at once, in a dedicated freeze
Never, since they keep working
Only after the next rebrand lands
On contact, when a squad is already editing them
items.explanation: Opportunistic migration avoids a roadmap freeze.

items.prompt: What must new screens do?
choices: Copy a nearby screen's styles
Use the library from day one
Wait until all old screens migrate
Pick their own colors, then align
items.explanation: New work should not add to the old problem.

items.prompt: Which two measures are tracked together?
choices: Adoption and visual-inconsistency incidents
Page views and shopper locations
Server cost and response time
Commit count and file size
items.explanation: Together they show the system paying off.

items.prompt: In the demo's model, incidents per month at 10% adoption?
items.explanation: The model starts at 14 incidents a month at 10% adoption.

items.prompt: In the demo's model, incidents per month at 95% adoption, rounded to 0.1?
items.explanation: The line falls toward the 1.5 floor, reaching 2.2 at 95%.

items.prompt: A manager proposes freezing the roadmap for a six-week migration. What is the alternative?
choices: Accept the freeze, because no rollout of this kind can ever be done in stages at all
Migrate only the screens nobody has touched in a long while to be safe
Publish tokens first, then migrate old screens on contact beside feature work
Skip components and instead publish a larger color palette for squads
items.explanation: Staged, opportunistic migration keeps feature work moving and still converges.
items.reference:
Rollout order
1️⃣ tokens from values in use
2️⃣ highest-collision components
3️⃣ migrate on contact
4️⃣ track adoption + incidents
Why: risk stays low early, and the evidence that funds year two accumulates as you go.

items.prompt: Who owns global and alias tokens?
choices: The design system team
Whichever squad edited them last
The newest engineer on each squad
The shoppers who use the checkout
items.explanation: Those layers fan out to everything.

items.prompt: Who may propose a new component?
choices: Only the design system team
Only the engineering director
Any squad
Only shoppers via a survey
items.explanation: Proposals stay open.

items.prompt: Who merges component changes?
choices: The squad that proposed it
The design system team
Whoever deploys first
An automated random vote
items.explanation: One merging team keeps one reviewer.

items.prompt: What is an RFC in this setting?
choices: A secret change made after hours
A bug ticket for the checkout screen
A color swatch printed on paper
A short written proposal visible to every squad
items.explanation: It makes a big change visible before it ships.

items.prompt: How are breaking changes released?
choices: Swapped silently overnight
Deprecated with a warning for one full release cycle
Kept hidden until squads complain
Applied only on weekends
items.explanation: Old usage keeps working while squads adjust.

items.prompt: Why is changing a global token slow on purpose?
choices: One edit fans out to everything below it
Global tokens are written in a hard language
The design team dislikes making changes
Tokens can only be edited once a year
items.explanation: High blast radius earns a higher bar.

items.prompt: What happens if five squads edit Button directly?
choices: Button becomes faster for every squad
The tokens get deleted by the build
Drift returns, now inside the shared library
Each squad gets its own safe copy
items.explanation: Without a gate the shared place becomes another place to drift.

items.prompt: From a squad's view, the component library is a...
choices: private file only its own squad owns
temporary draft that nobody depends on
decoration used only in marketing
dependency it did not choose to break
items.explanation: Squads build on it, so changes must respect that.

items.prompt: A squad wants to tweak blue.500 for their feature. What is the right route?
choices: Edit it directly, because their own feature is the only place it is used now
Create a hidden duplicate token and point their feature at the duplicate
Write an RFC, since a global change reaches every screen and needs review
Wait for the next rebrand and then edit the value without telling anyone
items.explanation: Global edits fan out to every consumer, so they need visibility first.
items.reference:
Who may do what
🏛️ global + alias: system team, via RFC
💡 any squad: propose
✅ system team: merges
⏳ breaking change: warn for one release cycle
Why: one reviewer sees every change in context, while open proposals keep the system useful.
items.learnMore:
Intentional bottleneck

The merge gate does the job the missing shared Button once did: it catches the sixth blue before it ships. Deprecation treats the library as a dependency squads did not choose to break.

Common mistake

Letting every squad edit the shared library directly.
items.reflection: Where in your own work does 'anyone proposes, one person merges' keep a shared thing coherent, and where would it only slow people down?
